newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Fireworks paint the sky red as HK sees in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Fireworks paint the sky red as HK sees in 1997.

text.p: Fireworks painted the night sky red as Hong Kong saw in 1997, the year when the wealthy British colony is destined, like it or not, to become a part of China once again.

Bagpipes skirled, kilts swirled, car drivers pounded their horns and black-jeaned Chinese teenageers screamed in a welcome to a new year in which more than 150 years of British rule will end at midnight on June 30 when the red flag of China rises over this community of 6.3 million.

While the world marked just another countdown on the road to the millenium, Hong Kong contemplated a historic change. "1997" is branded in the collective memory as shorthand for the handover to Communist China now just 181 days away.

For a brief few hours, hedonism triumphed, reinforced by the heady fizz of champagne bubbles and the cordite crack of fireworks, relegating concerns about the future to the backburner as Hong Kong's muscular party spirit reigned defiant.

The Scottish ghosts of the founders of the Jardine Matheson trading empire, who urged the British government into the Opium Wars with China which led to the seizing of Hong Kong in 1841, were recalled when the Jardine gun boomed out at midnight.
Across on the north side of the bay a fireworks display watched by tens of thousands sounded in counterpoint.

The Jardine gun has a special place in Hong Kong folklore. Early Jardine merchant princes fired a military-style salute to mark the arrival of the company chairmain in a tea clipper in the last century to the ire of the British military.

Their punishment was to mark every noon with gunfire -- a custom gleefully siezed on by the founder's descendents who to this day signal eight bells -- or noon -- with cannon fire -- and aim to continue after the handover.
"Of course it will continue," said a senior Jardine official. "Why not?"
Crowds climbed walls to watch the gun being fired at midnight. Barely a beat later, car horns echoed forth.
Foreign eyes grew misty as Hong Kong's once influential Scottish expatriates proudly heard the asynchronous notes of Auld Lang Syne from a lone piper echoing across the China sea.

But the sounds of the bagpipes failed to blot out the undercurrent of concern. Outside the floodlight domes of Hong Kong's Legislative Council, defiant pro-democracy politicians congregated to vow no surrender.
They counted down the seconds to the New Year and pledged they would not surrender to what they regard as efforts by Beijing to roll back freedoms and democracy.
"Keep my seat warm," shouted Martin Lee, leader of Hong Kong's largest party, the Democracy Party, which is due to be kicked out of the Legislative Council at the handover.

China aims to dissolve the elected legislature and replace it with an appointed body when it takes over next July 1, in a stroke undoing electoral reforms spearheaded by the 28th and last British governor of Hong Kong, Chris Patten, passed in the twilight of British rule.
A small but vocal group of demonstrators gathered outside the offices of China's de facto representative office in Hong Kong, demanding the release of dissidents jailed by Beijing.

In Hong Kong's nightclub district, police threw a a tight but low-key and polite cordon around the popular cobbled-street quarter of Lan Kwai Fong, scene of a 1992 New Year tragedy when almost two dozen young revellers were crushed to death on the slippery slopes as crowds got out of hand.
Aerosols were banned and youngsters forbidden to spray the cobbles with beer and fizzy wine but spirits still rang high.
"Happy New Year," bubbled a shaven-headed British teenager to a twenty-something leather-clad Chinese rocker as she offered him a sip from her bottle of sparkling Australian wine.
He in turn proffered a sip from a vintage year.
